name: Blonde Ale
title: Blonde Ale: Style Guide | Craft Beer School
desc: Blonde ale explained: a light, soft, gently hopped ale that converts lager drinkers. Taste, serving, Indian food pairings and local examples.
tagline: The friendly ale. Light, bready and quietly made, it is often the beer a brewpub sells most of.
tastes:
Blonde ale is pale, soft and easy. The malt gives a light bready or crackery sweetness, sometimes a hint of honey, and the hops sit in the background with a little floral or citrus lift. Bitterness is gentle. The finish is clean and fairly dry, so it never cloys.

It grew up in American brewpubs, where brewers needed an ale for customers who mostly drank lager. Fermented warm with a clean ale yeast, it is quicker to make than a lager and can be on tap in a couple of weeks, yet it drinks almost as crisply. Some brewers use a German or Czech pilsner malt for a slightly richer bread note, others add a touch of wheat for a fuller head.

There is nothing loud about it, and that is the point. A blonde ale shows whether a brewer can make a clean beer with nowhere to hide. Any off note, a whiff of butter from diacetyl or a solvent edge from a hot ferment, stands out straight away in a beer this light.

profile.look: Straw to light gold, clear, with a white head of moderate size.
profile.aroma_flavour: Light bread, cracker and a little honey from the malt, with low floral or citrus hop notes. Few or no fruity yeast esters.
profile.mouthfeel: Light to medium-light body, medium to lively carbonation, a soft and clean finish with low bitterness.
profile.ingredients: Pale or pilsner malt, sometimes a little wheat or light crystal, a modest charge of American or noble hops and a clean ale yeast. Rice is a natural fit.

in_india: This is the style that brings lager drinkers into a brewpub and keeps them there, which is why many Indian brewpubs keep one on all year. It suits Indian heat well: light, cold and low in bitterness, it works on a Chennai afternoon or a crowded wedding lawn. Indian brewers have also used basmati and other local rice in the grist, which keeps the body light and adds a faint aroma of its own. Fresh from the tap is best, as light beers show stale flavours quickly.

pairings.why: The crisp dosa and the bready malt meet half way and the low bitterness leaves the potato filling alone.
A light, clean beer lets the pepper and coconut oil come through instead of covering them.
The gentle sweetness matches the steamed batter and the carbonation clears the tempering of mustard seed and chilli.
The beer is light enough to sit next to a delicate milk sweet and the honey note in the malt echoes the saffron syrup.
